results.title: Morris, T.P., Kahan, B.C. and White, I.R. (2014) Choosing Sensitivity Analyses for Randomised Trials Principles. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 14, Article No. 11. - References
results.content: *   TITLE: Evaluating Utility of Machine Learning-Based Imputation Methods to Account for Attrition in Multi-Stage Epilepsy Prevalence Surveys. KEYWORDS: Prevalence, Missing Data, Machine Learning, Multiple Imputation, Inverse Probability Weighting, Attrition, Epilepsy, Population-Based Studies. While strategies to reduce attrition should ideally be implemented during the study design phase, they remain common in real-world research, necessitating statistical methods to address them. This study examines four ML-based imputation methods to account for attrition and compares them with conventional MI and IPW in a two-stage epilepsy population-based prevalence survey involving 56,425 participants. k-nearest neighbor (KNN) and sequential KNN (sKNN) performed similarly to MI under MAR but exhibited less bias than MI and IPW when data were MNAR. While MI is still the most preferred for missing data assuming MAR, ML methods, particularly sKNN and KNN demonstrated potential for addressing attrition when data are MNAR. Future research should explore ML methods in various study designs and consider integrating ML into the very robust MI framework to improve prediction accuracy for missing data due to attrition.

results.title: Unmeasured confounding | Causal Inference Class Notes
results.content: * Unmeasured confounding is a major challenge in causal inference that occurs when there are variables that affect both the treatment and outcome but are not included in the analysis. * When unmeasured confounders are present, the observed association between the treatment and outcome may not reflect the true causal relationship. * Positive confounding occurs when the unmeasured confounder is positively associated with both the treatment and outcome, leading to an overestimation of the causal effect. * Negative confounding occurs when the unmeasured confounder is negatively associated with either the treatment or outcome, leading to an underestimation of the causal effect. * Instrumental variables (IVs) are a method for addressing unmeasured confounding by identifying variables that are associated with the treatment but not the outcome. * When these assumptions are met, the IV can be used to estimate the causal effect of the treatment on the outcome, even in the presence of unmeasured confounding.
